\chapter{Ahí, Allí --- The Other Two Places}
\label{ch:ahi-alli}
\hlchaptermodality{251}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say where something is, on any of the three sides.}

I can say where something is, on any of the three sides.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ahí · allí]{ahí · allí — the other two places}

\label{lesson:ES-C65-ahi-alli}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Aquí} — here. You have had it a long time, on its own.

And you know three pointing words: \emph{este}, \emph{ese}, \emph{aquel}. The places work the same way, and they have been waiting for their other two.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one for one}]
Say them: \emph{\textbf{aquí}}, by me. \emph{\textbf{Ahí}}, by you. \emph{\textbf{Allí}}, away from us both.

They line up with the pointing words exactly:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{este libro} & \emph{\textbf{aquí}} & by me \\
\emph{ese libro} & \emph{\textbf{ahí}} & by you \\
\emph{aquel libro} & \emph{\textbf{allí}} & by neither \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So this is not a new system to learn. It is the \textbf{same} system, answering the same question — whose side is it on — with a word for the place instead of a word for the thing.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
All three carry a written accent, and all three carry it for the same reason: each is stressed on its \textbf{last} syllable, and each ends in a vowel, where Spanish would otherwise stress the one before.

\emph{A-QUÍ}. \emph{A-HÍ}. \emph{A-LLÍ}. Say them and you can hear the beat landing at the end every time.

English gets by with two — \emph{here} and \emph{there} — and patches the third on when it must: \emph{over there}. Spanish keeps all three separate, exactly as it does with the pointing words.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aquí}, \emph{ahí}, \emph{allí}
  \item \emph{este libro aquí}, \emph{ese libro ahí}, \emph{aquel libro allí}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which place word sits on the listener's side? (\emph{\textbf{Ahí}}.)

And why do all three take an accent? (Each is stressed on its \textbf{last} syllable.)
\end{tcolorbox}
